entries.transcript: Right, the decoupling argument. The claim is that you can keep growing the economy while emissions fall, and there are countries where that has genuinely happened, so it's not a lie. But when you put the consumption back in, when you count the stuff that got made somewhere else and shipped in, most of that gap closes. And the bit that's left is nowhere near the rate you'd need. So decoupling isn't happening at anything like the speed the plans assume, and every plan I've read still has growth sitting in the base case as if it were a law of physics.
entries.title: decoupling isn't happening
entries.summary: Absolute decoupling of growth from emissions is not occurring at the required rate.

entries.transcript: But you can't degrowth your way to a grid. That's the thing I keep running into. Every version of the transition needs an enormous amount of building — cable, turbines, storage, heat pumps in nine hundred thousand houses a year — and building is materials and materials is emissions and it all lands in the next fifteen years, which is exactly the window we said mattered. So there's a build phase where the numbers go the wrong way before they go the right way, and I don't think I have an honest answer for that.
entries.title: still need the build
entries.summary: The transition itself requires a materially intensive build phase.

entries.transcript: Went looking for what a data centre actually costs to run and the water is the part nobody puts in the press release. Cooling. Millions of litres a year, sited more often than not in places that are already dry, because dry is cheap and cheap is where you build. And the local authority signs it off for the jobs, which turn out to be about forty people once it's up. Forty. Against a water table.
entries.title: a datacentre drinks
entries.summary: Data centre siting trades local water for a small number of jobs.

entries.transcript: The WMO number came out. They're calling it "1.43 degrees above pre industrial temperatures" and the last ten years are the ten warmest on record, which I already knew and it still landed differently written down. And I noticed my own reaction, which was to immediately start thinking about whether the measurement window was fair. That's what I did with it. I went looking for a technicality.
entries.title: one point four three
entries.summary: The 2025 WMO figure, and a first reaction of looking for a technicality.

entries.transcript: The targets have become a ritual. Nobody in the room believes the 2030 one is going to be met, and everybody keeps planning against it, and both of those things are true at the same time and nobody says so out loud. It's not lying exactly. It's that the target stopped being a forecast and became a thing you affirm, and affirming it is now the work. Missing it doesn't cost anything, because the next target is already published.
entries.title: targets became ritual
entries.summary: Climate targets function as affirmation rather than forecast.

entries.transcript: I think the word is doing damage. Degrowth. Every time I use it in a room the argument stops being about throughput and starts being about whether I want people to be poorer, and I lose forty minutes I'm not getting back. And the counter is that softening the word is exactly how the thing gets defanged, that's what happened to sustainability, it got so agreeable it stopped meaning anything. So the word is either load-bearing or a liability and I genuinely cannot tell which.
entries.title: the word does damage
entries.summary: Whether the term degrowth costs more in argument than it gains in clarity.

entries.transcript: Limits are not austerity and I need to be able to say this in one sentence. Austerity is less for the people who already have least, decided by people who won't feel it. Limits are a ceiling on throughput, and the entire question of who gets what underneath that ceiling is still open — it can be more equal under a limit than it is now. They're opposite in who they cost. The reason they get confused is that both of them say the word less.
entries.title: limits are not austerity
entries.summary: Distinguishing a throughput ceiling from austerity by who bears the cost.

entries.transcript: The bit that gets left out of the AI energy argument is ownership. Everyone's arguing about how many watts a query costs, which is a real question, but the models are owned in about four places and rented to everyone else, and the countries hosting the compute are mostly not the countries deciding what it's for. That's the same shape as every extraction arrangement I've ever read about. The energy argument is the one we're allowed to have.
entries.title: who owns the model
entries.summary: The ownership question underneath the AI energy debate.

entries.transcript: I stopped flying two years ago and I still don't know what it was for. It's about a tonne a year, which against anything structural is nothing, and I know that, I've done the arithmetic more than once. But I didn't stop because of the arithmetic. And my sister's wedding is in March and she's not going to say anything about it and that's somehow worse than if she did.
entries.title: stopped flying

entries.transcript: Housekeeping. Move the climate feeds off the reader that got acquired. Find where the WMO release actually publishes rather than reading it third hand. Cancel the storage tier I stopped using in June.
entries.title: feeds to move
entries.summary: A short list of tooling and subscription changes.
actionItems: Move the climate feeds off the reader that got acquired
Cancel the storage tier I stopped using in June

entries.transcript: So I've moved off it properly this time, not the half move where you keep the account and check it. And the honest bit is that it's quieter and I miss it, and the two things aren't in tension, they're just both true. What I actually got back is that nobody is optimising what I see. Nobody's deciding the order. It turns out the order was most of what I disliked and I couldn't see that from inside it.
entries.title: left the platform
entries.summary: Moving off a mainstream platform and what changed afterwards.

entries.transcript: The contract is the point, not the software. Everyone argues about whether the tool works, is it accurate, does it discriminate, all of which matters, but the thing that actually happened is a company now sits inside the data flow of a public service and the exit cost goes up every year it stays. In ten years you don't choose whether to renew. That was decided at signing and nobody voted on it.
entries.title: the contract is the point
entries.summary: Procurement lock-in as the real mechanism, ahead of software quality.

entries.transcript: Reading Digital Degrowth. The line that stuck was about the sector being sold as immaterial while running on the most material supply chain we have — cobalt, water, land, the lot. And I've been making a softer version of that argument for months without the vocabulary for it. Slightly annoying to find your own thought better expressed by someone who did the reading.
entries.title: the book got there first
entries.summary: Notes on Digital Degrowth and its framing of the sector as material.
attributedQuotes: the sector being sold as immaterial while running on the most material supply chain we have — cobalt, water, land, the lot

entries.transcript: The consultation closed and the decision was in the papers before it opened. Six weeks of a form nobody read, and the honest version would have been to just say we've decided, here's why. Instead we all performed the process. And I filled it in anyway, which is the part I'm annoyed about.
entries.title: consultation was decided
entries.summary: A local consultation run after the decision was made.

entries.transcript: The dumping report finally landed and the timeline is the story. They knew for years. Not suspected, knew, and the sites are exactly where you'd expect, which is next to the people least able to make it expensive for anyone. And it'll be a fine, and the fine will be smaller than the saving.
entries.title: they knew for years
entries.summary: A waste dumping report where the timeline is the substance.

entries.transcript: Src blocks still aren't publishing. Renders fine locally, comes out empty on the built site, so it's something in the export step and not the config I've spent two evenings on. Try the other exporter before I lose another night to this.
entries.title: src blocks not publishing
entries.summary: A publishing bug in the site export step.

entries.transcript: There was a heron at the weir again this morning, same spot as last week, and I stood there longer than I meant to. It didn't move the entire time. I've walked past that weir maybe four hundred times.
entries.title: heron at the weir

entries.transcript: The sanctions argument keeps getting made as though the pain lands where the decision is made, and it doesn't, it lands about four rungs down from anyone who could change anything. Which doesn't make them always wrong, but it does mean the case has to be made on something other than pressure, and it almost never is.
entries.title: sanctions miss the target
entries.summary: Who actually bears the cost of economic sanctions.

entries.transcript: Fourth loaf and it's still coming out dense. Starter's lively, oven's hot enough, so it's the shaping or it's the proving and I can't tell which because I changed both. Which is the actual lesson and it's not about bread.
entries.title: the loaf keeps failing
entries.summary: A run of failed bakes and one variable too many.

entries.transcript: Third week on the same record and I'm not bored of it, which never happens. I think it's that it doesn't resolve. Every time I expect the thing to land it goes somewhere adjacent instead.
entries.title: same album all week

edges.question: February says growth cannot be decoupled fast enough; March says the transition needs a large build regardless. Does the build get counted inside the growth you rejected, or outside it?
The build phase was argued as a cost worth paying for the grid. Does a data centre qualify as that kind of build, or is it the other kind?
Both entries say the plans assume something nobody expects to hold. Is that one objection stated twice, or two different failures?
March treats the build as something we collectively need. This entry says the thing being built is owned in four places. Who is the we in the March entry?
April describes going looking for a technicality. Is the argument about the word doing the same thing in a different register?
Both entries locate the problem in who sets the order rather than in the artefact itself. Is that the same objection, or does one of them let the artefact off too easily?
One entry says the fine will be smaller than the saving; the other says the exit cost only ever rises. Do those two mechanisms have the same fix?

questions.text: The entry rejects growth in the base case but keeps the same energy demand curve underneath it. Is the demand curve also an assumption?
questions.spanQuote: every plan I've read still has growth sitting in the base case

questions.text: You say you have no honest answer for the build phase. What would an answer have to contain for you to accept it?
questions.spanQuote: I don't think I have an honest answer for that

questions.text: You call the energy argument the one we're allowed to have. Allowed by whom, and what would asking the other question cost?
questions.spanQuote: The energy argument is the one we're allowed to have

questions.text: If missing the target costs nothing, what were you relying on the target to do?
You say nobody voted on it. What would a vote have needed to be about for it to have mattered?
questions.spanQuote: That was decided at signing and nobody voted on it

questions.text: The entry rests on the distribution under the ceiling still being open. Open in principle, or open in practice?
questions.spanQuote: the entire question of who gets what underneath that ceiling is still open

questions.text: The entry treats the softer version and the book's version as the same argument. What did the vocabulary let the book say that the softer one could not?
questions.spanQuote: I've been making a softer version of that argument for months without the vocabulary for it

questions.text: The entry says the case has to rest on something other than pressure. What would that other thing be?
questions.spanQuote: the case has to be made on something other than pressure
